title: Where a household stands relative to its neighborhood is linked to how far it moves
source_unit: Census CES Working Paper 26-20 using restricted-use American Community Survey data and multinomial mobility models
geography: United States; census tracts, counties, households, and short- versus long-distance residential mobility

observations.period: Restricted-use ACS residential mobility analysis; paper published March 2026

denominator.unit: household-level multinomial mobility analysis using restricted-use American Community Survey data

neighborhood_status.value: tract median family income relative to demographically similar reference neighborhoods

individual_status.value: household income rank within its tract

low_neighborhood_high_individual.value: disadvantaged neighborhood status paired with high individual status increases within-county mobility

high_neighborhood_low_individual.value: low individual status in high-status neighborhoods heightens mobility

distance_pattern.value: neighborhood status primarily shapes short-distance mobility; status mismatch is linked to both within- and between-county mobility patterns

interpretation.value: patterns are consistent with spatial assimilation and relative deprivation mechanisms

observations.method: The authors construct contextual and positional status measures from restricted-use ACS data and estimate multinomial logistic models for within-county and between-county moves.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census CES working paper and not a Census Bureau endorsement. The reported model relationships do not establish that status mismatch caused a move, identify the household's reason for moving, or measure housing quality, cost, discrimination, belonging, safety, or later wellbeing.
observations.subgroup: Households classified by tract status, within-tract income rank, and short- versus long-distance residential mobility; race, family, tenure, and life-course mechanisms require separate analysis.
observations.counterinterpretation: Moves may reflect rent, jobs, family, school, safety, discrimination, illness, or housing supply rather than status comparison. A move can be an improvement, forced displacement, strategic adaptation, or an unresolved transition; the same status pattern can contain different experiences.

related_sources.claim: The official paper provides the status definitions, mobility categories, multinomial models, and theoretical interpretation.

boundary: This record adds a relative-status-to-residential-mobility pathway. It does not establish causal status effects, household motives, housing affordability, discrimination, belonging, safety, wellbeing, or whether moving represents exit, opportunity, or displacement.
